But I want the right to look after you.”"}, {"paragraph": 4, "text": "“That’s what I want,” said the girl wistfully. “Some one who’ll be good to me.”"}, {"paragraph": 5, "text": "“Sure thing. Then I guess that’s all fixed up, and I’ll see the archbishop about a special license to-morrow morning.”"}, {"paragraph": 6, "text": "“Oh, Julius!”"}, {"paragraph": 7, "text": "“Well, I don’t want to hustle you any, Jane, but there’s no sense in waiting about.”"}, {"paragraph": 8, "text": "But a small hand was slipped into his."}, {"paragraph": 9, "text": "“I love you now, Julius,” said Jane Finn. “I loved you that first moment in the car when the bullet grazed your cheek....”"}, {"paragraph": 10, "text": "Five minutes later Jane murmured softly:"}, {"paragraph": 11, "text": "“Is it such a very long way from the _Savoy_ to the _Ritz?_”"}, {"paragraph": 12, "text": "“It depends how you go,” explained Julius unblushingly. “We’re going by way of Regent’s Park! The only reason I had the supper at the _Savoy_ was so that I could drive you home. You and Tuppence have been sticking together like Siamese twins. I guess another day of it would have driven me and Beresford stark staring mad!”"}, {"paragraph": 13, "text": "“Oh. Is he----?”"}, {"paragraph": 14, "text": "“Of course he is. Head over ears.”"}, {"paragraph": 15, "text": "“I thought so,” said Jane thoughtfully."}, {"paragraph": 16, "text": "“Why?”"}, {"paragraph": 17, "text": "“From all the things Tuppence didn’t say!”"}, {"paragraph": 18, "text": "The Young Adventurers were sitting bolt upright in a taxi which, with a singular lack of originality, was also returning to the _Ritz_ via Regent’s Park."}, {"paragraph": 19, "text": "They were tongue-tied--paralysed. All the old _camaraderie_ was gone."}, {"paragraph": 20, "text": "“I like Julius,” essayed Tuppence."}, {"paragraph": 21, "text": "Tommy was suddenly galvanized into life."}, {"paragraph": 22, "text": "“You’re not going to marry him, do you hear?” he said dictatorially. “I forbid it.”"}, {"paragraph": 23, "text": "“Oh!” said Tuppence meekly. “He doesn’t want to marry me--he really only asked me out of kindness. He’s head over ears in love with Jane.”"}, {"paragraph": 24, "text": "“She’ll do for him very nicely,” said Tommy condescendingly."}, {"paragraph": 25, "text": "“But I suppose you prefer sterling worth,” said Tuppence demurely."}, {"paragraph": 26, "text": "“I--oh, dash it all, Tuppence, you know!”"}, {"paragraph": 27, "text": "“By the way,” said Tuppence, hastily creating a diversion, “are you going to accept Mr. Carter’s offer of a Government job, or take a richly remunerated post on Julius’s ranch?”"}, {"paragraph": 28, "text": "“I shall stick to the old ship, I think. I feel you’d be more at home in London.”"}, {"paragraph": 29, "text": "“I don’t see where I come in.”"}, {"paragraph": 30, "text": "“I do,” said Tommy positively."}, {"paragraph": 31, "text": "“We’re going to get a cheque each,” observed Tuppence. “Mr. Carter told me so.”"}, {"paragraph": 32, "text": "“Did you ask how much?” inquired Tommy sarcastically."}, {"paragraph": 33, "text": "“Yes,” said Tuppence triumphantly. “But I shan’t tell you.”"}, {"paragraph": 34, "text": "“Think of buying old furniture,” said Tuppence dreamily, “and a divan with lots of cushions.”"}, {"paragraph": 35, "text": "“Hold hard,” said Tommy. “What’s all this for?”"}, {"paragraph": 36, "text": "“Possibly a house--but I think a flat.”"}, {"paragraph": 37, "text": "“Whose flat?”"}, {"paragraph": 38, "text": "“You think I mind saying it, but I don’t in the least! _Ours_, so there!”"}, {"paragraph": 39, "text": "“You darling!” cried Tommy, his arms tightly round her. “I owe you something for the relentless way you’ve squashed me whenever I’ve tried to be sentimental.”"}, {"paragraph": 40, "text": "“You haven’t really proposed now,” pointed out Tuppence. “But after listening to a rotten one like Julius’s, I’m inclined to let you off.”"}, {"paragraph": 41, "text": "“You won’t be able to get out of marrying me, so don’t you think it.”"}, {"paragraph": 42, "text": "“What fun it will be,” responded Tuppence. “Marriage is called a haven, and a state of bondage. But do you know what I think it is?”"}, {"paragraph": 43, "text": "“What?”"}, {"paragraph": 44, "text": "“A sport!”"}, {"paragraph": 45, "text": "“And a damned good sport too,” said Tommy."}], "002.source": [{"paragraph": 1, "text": "“TOMMY, old thing!”"}, {"paragraph": 2, "text": "“Tuppence, old bean!”"}, {"paragraph": 3, "text": "The two young people greeted each other affectionately, and momentarily\nblocked the Dover Street Tube exit in doing so. The adjective “old”\n was misleading. Their united ages would certainly not have totalled\nforty-five."}, {"paragraph": 4, "text": "“Not seen you for simply centuries,” continued the young man. “Where are\nyou off to? Come and chew a bun with me. We’re getting a bit unpopular\nhere--blocking the gangway as it were. Let’s get out of it.”"}, {"paragraph": 5, "text": "The girl assenting, they started walking down Dover Street towards\nPiccadilly."}, {"paragraph": 6, "text": "“Now then,” said Tommy, “where shall we go?”"}, {"paragraph": 7, "text": "The very faint anxiety which underlay his tone did not escape the astute\nears of Miss Prudence Cowley, known to her intimate friends for some\nmysterious reason as “Tuppence.” She pounced at once."}, {"paragraph": 8, "text": "“Tommy, you’re stony!”"}, {"paragraph": 9, "text": "“Not a bit of it,” declared Tommy unconvincingly. “Rolling in cash.”"}, {"paragraph": 10, "text": "“You always were a shocking liar,” said Tuppence severely, “though you\ndid once persuade Sister Greenbank that the doctor had ordered you beer\nas a tonic, but forgotten to write it on the chart. Do you remember?”"}, {"paragraph": 11, "text": "Tommy chuckled."}, {"paragraph": 12, "text": "“I should think I did! Wasn’t the old cat in a rage when she found\nout? Not that she was a bad sort really, old Mother Greenbank! Good old\nhospital--demobbed like everything else, I suppose?”"}, {"paragraph": 13, "text": "Tuppence sighed."}, {"paragraph": 14, "text": "“Yes. You too?”"}, {"paragraph": 15, "text": "Tommy nodded."}, {"paragraph": 16, "text": "“Two months ago.”"}, {"paragraph": 17, "text": "“Gratuity?” hinted Tuppence."}, {"paragraph": 18, "text": "“Spent.”"}, {"paragraph": 19, "text": "“Oh, Tommy!”"}, {"paragraph": 20, "text": "“No, old thing, not in riotous dissipation. No such luck! The cost of\nliving--ordinary plain, or garden living nowadays is, I assure you, if\nyou do not know----”"}, {"paragraph": 21, "text": "“My dear child,” interrupted Tuppence, “there is nothing I do _not_ know\nabout the cost of living. Here we are at Lyons’, and we will each of us\npay for our own. That’s it!” And Tuppence led the way upstairs."}, {"paragraph": 22, "text": "The place was full, and they wandered about looking for a table,\ncatching odds and ends of conversation as they did so."}, {"paragraph": 23, "text": "“And--do you know, she sat down and _cried_ when I told her she couldn’t\nhave the flat after all.” “It was simply a _bargain_, my dear! Just like\nthe one Mabel Lewis brought from Paris----”"}, {"paragraph": 24, "text": "“Funny scraps one does overhear,” murmured Tommy. “I passed two Johnnies\nin the street to-day talking about some one called Jane Finn. Did you\never hear such a name?”"}, {"paragraph": 25, "text": "But at that moment two elderly ladies rose and collected parcels, and\nTuppence deftly ensconced herself in one of the vacant seats."}, {"paragraph": 26, "text": "Tommy ordered tea and buns. Tuppence ordered tea and buttered toast."}, {"paragraph": 27, "text": "“And mind the tea comes in separate teapots,” she added severely."}, {"paragraph": 28, "text": "Tommy sat down opposite her. His bared head revealed a shock\nof exquisitely slicked-back red hair. His face was pleasantly\nugly--nondescript, yet unmistakably the face of a gentleman and a\nsportsman. His brown suit was well cut, but perilously near the end of\nits tether."}, {"paragraph": 29, "text": "They were an essentially modern-looking couple as they sat there.\nTuppence had no claim to beauty, but there was character and charm in\nthe elfin lines of her little face, with its determined chin and large,\nwide-apart grey eyes that looked mistily out from under straight, black\nbrows. She wore a small bright green toque over her black bobbed hair,\nand her extremely short and rather shabby skirt revealed a pair of\nuncommonly dainty ankles. Her appearance presented a valiant attempt at\nsmartness."}, {"paragraph": 30, "text": "The tea came at last, and Tuppence, rousing herself from a fit of\nmeditation, poured it out."}, {"paragraph": 31, "text": "“Now then,” said Tommy, taking a large bite of bun, “let’s get\nup-to-date. Remember, I haven’t seen you since that time in hospital in\n1916.”"}, {"paragraph": 32, "text": "“Very well.” Tuppence helped herself liberally to buttered toast.\n“Abridged biography of Miss Prudence Cowley, fifth daughter of\nArchdeacon Cowley of Little Missendell, Suffolk. Miss Cowley left the\ndelights (and drudgeries) of her home life early in the war and came up\nto London, where she entered an officers’ hospital. First month: Washed\nup six hundred and forty-eight plates every day. Second month: Promoted\nto drying aforesaid plates. Third month: Promoted to peeling potatoes.\nFourth month: Promoted to cutting bread and butter. Fifth month:\nPromoted one floor up to duties of wardmaid with mop and pail. Sixth\nmonth: Promoted to waiting at table. Seventh month: Pleasing appearance\nand nice manners so striking that am promoted to waiting on the Sisters!\nEighth month: Slight check in career. Sister Bond ate Sister Westhaven’s\negg! Grand row! Wardmaid clearly to blame! Inattention in such important\nmatters cannot be too highly censured. Mop and pail again! How are the\nmighty fallen! Ninth month: Promoted to sweeping out wards, where I\nfound a friend of my childhood in Lieutenant Thomas Beresford (bow,\nTommy!), whom I had not seen for five long years. The meeting was\naffecting! Tenth month: Reproved by matron for visiting the pictures in\ncompany with one of the patients, namely: the aforementioned Lieutenant\nThomas Beresford. Eleventh and twelfth months: Parlourmaid duties\nresumed with entire success. At the end of the year left hospital in a\nblaze of glory. After that, the talented Miss Cowley drove successively\na trade delivery van, a motor-lorry and a general! The last was the\npleasantest. He was quite a young general!”"}, {"paragraph": 33, "text": "“What blighter was that?” inquired Tommy. “Perfectly sickening the way\nthose brass hats drove from the War Office to the _Savoy_, and from the\n_Savoy_ to the War Office!”"}, {"paragraph": 34, "text": "“I’ve forgotten his name now,” confessed Tuppence. “To resume, that was\nin a way the apex of my career. I next entered a Government office. We\nhad several very enjoyable tea parties. I had intended to become a\nland girl, a postwoman, and a bus conductress by way of rounding off\nmy career--but the Armistice intervened! I clung to the office with the\ntrue limpet touch for many long months, but, alas, I was combed out at\nlast. Since then I’ve been looking for a job. Now then--your turn.”"}, {"paragraph": 35, "text": "“There’s not so much promotion in mine,” said Tommy regretfully, “and a\ngreat deal less variety. I went out to France again, as you know. Then\nthey sent me to Mesopotamia, and I got wounded for the second time,\nand went into hospital out there. Then I got stuck in Egypt till the\nArmistice happened, kicked my heels there some time longer, and, as I\ntold you, finally got demobbed. And, for ten long, weary months I’ve\nbeen job hunting! There aren’t any jobs! And, if there were, they\nwouldn’t give ‘em to me. What good am I? What do I know about business?\nNothing.”"}, {"paragraph": 36, "text": "Tuppence nodded gloomily."}, {"paragraph": 37, "text": "“What about the colonies?” she suggested."}, {"paragraph": 38, "text": "Tommy shook his head."}, {"paragraph": 39, "text": "“I shouldn’t like the colonies--and I’m perfectly certain they wouldn’t\nlike me!”"}, {"paragraph": 40, "text": "“Rich relations?”"}, {"paragraph": 41, "text": "Again Tommy shook his head."}, {"paragraph": 42, "text": "“Oh, Tommy, not even a great-aunt?”"}, {"paragraph": 43, "text": "“I’ve got an old uncle who’s more or less rolling, but he’s no good.”"}, {"paragraph": 44, "text": "“Why not?”"}, {"paragraph": 45, "text": "“Wanted to adopt me once. I refused.”"}, {"paragraph": 46, "text": "“I think I remember hearing about it,” said Tuppence slowly. “You\nrefused because of your mother----”"}, {"paragraph": 47, "text": "Tommy flushed."}, {"paragraph": 48, "text": "“Yes, it would have been a bit rough on the mater. As you know, I was\nall she had. Old boy hated her--wanted to get me away from her. Just a\nbit of spite.”"}, {"paragraph": 49, "text": "“Your mother’s dead, isn’t she?” said Tuppence gently."}, {"paragraph": 50, "text": "Tommy nodded."}, {"paragraph": 51, "text": "Tuppence’s large grey eyes looked misty."}, {"paragraph": 52, "text": "“You’re a good sort, Tommy. I always knew it.”"}, {"paragraph": 53, "text": "“Rot!” said Tommy hastily. “Well, that’s my position. I’m just about\ndesperate.”"}, {"paragraph": 54, "text": "“So am I! I’ve hung out as long as I could. I’ve touted round. I’ve\nanswered advertisements. I’ve tried every mortal blessed thing. I’ve\nscrewed and saved and pinched! But it’s no good. I shall have to go\nhome!”"}, {"paragraph": 55, "text": "“Don’t you want to?”"}, {"paragraph": 56, "text": "“Of course I don’t want to! What’s the good of being sentimental?\nFather’s a dear--I’m awfully fond of him--but you’ve no idea how I worry\nhim! He has that delightful early Victorian view that short skirts and\nsmoking are immoral. You can imagine what a thorn in the flesh I am to\nhim! He just heaved a sigh of relief when the war took me off. You see,\nthere are seven of us at home. It’s awful! All housework and mothers’\nmeetings! I have always been the changeling. I don’t want to go back,\nbut--oh, Tommy, what else is there to do?”"}, {"paragraph": 57, "text": "Tommy shook his head sadly. There was a silence, and then Tuppence burst\nout:"}, {"paragraph": 58, "text": "“Money, money, money! I think about money morning, noon and night! I\ndare say it’s mercenary of me, but there it is!”"}, {"paragraph": 59, "text": "“Same here,” agreed Tommy with feeling."}, {"paragraph": 60, "text": "“I’ve thought over every imaginable way of getting it too,” continued\nTuppence. “There are only three! To be left it, to marry it, or to make\nit. First is ruled out. I haven’t got any rich elderly relatives. Any\nrelatives I have are in homes for decayed gentlewomen! I always help old\nladies over crossings, and pick up parcels for old gentlemen, in case\nthey should turn out to be eccentric millionaires. But not one of them\nhas ever asked me my name--and quite a lot never said ‘Thank you.’”"}, {"paragraph": 61, "text": "There was a pause."}, {"paragraph": 62, "text": "“Of course,” resumed Tuppence, “marriage is my best chance. I made up my\nmind to marry money when I was quite young. Any thinking girl would!\nI’m not sentimental, you know.” She paused. “Come now, you can’t say I’m\nsentimental,” she added sharply."}, {"paragraph": 63, "text": "“Certainly not,” agreed Tommy hastily. “No one would ever think of\nsentiment in connection with you.”"}, {"paragraph": 64, "text": "“That’s not very polite,” replied Tuppence. “But I dare say you mean it\nall right. Well, there it is! I’m ready and willing--but I never meet\nany rich men! All the boys I know are about as hard up as I am.”"}, {"paragraph": 65, "text": "“What about the general?” inquired Tommy."}, {"paragraph": 66, "text": "“I fancy he keeps a bicycle shop in time of peace,” explained Tuppence.\n“No, there it is! Now _you_ could marry a rich girl.”"}, {"paragraph": 67, "text": "“I’m like you. I don’t know any.”"}, {"paragraph": 68, "text": "“That doesn’t matter. You can always get to know one. Now, if I see a\nman in a fur coat come out of the _Ritz_ I can’t rush up to him and say:\n‘Look here, you’re rich. I’d like to know you.’”"}, {"paragraph": 69, "text": "“Do you suggest that I should do that to a similarly garbed female?”"}, {"paragraph": 70, "text": "“Don’t be silly. You tread on her foot, or pick up her handkerchief, or\nsomething like that. If she thinks you want to know her she’s flattered,\nand will manage it for you somehow.”"}, {"paragraph": 71, "text": "“You overrate my manly charms,” murmured Tommy."}, {"paragraph": 72, "text": "“On the other hand,” proceeded Tuppence, “my millionaire would probably\nrun for his life! No--marriage is fraught with difficulties. Remains--to\n_make_ money!”"}, {"paragraph": 73, "text": "“We’ve tried that, and failed,” Tommy reminded her."}, {"paragraph": 74, "text": "“We’ve tried all the orthodox ways, yes. But suppose we try the\nunorthodox. Tommy, let’s be adventurers!”"}, {"paragraph": 75, "text": "“Certainly,” replied Tommy cheerfully. “How do we begin?”"}, {"paragraph": 76, "text": "“That’s the difficulty. If we could make ourselves known, people might\nhire us to commit crimes for them.”"}, {"paragraph": 77, "text": "“Delightful,” commented Tommy. “Especially coming from a clergyman’s\ndaughter!”"}, {"paragraph": 78, "text": "“The moral guilt,” Tuppence pointed out, “would be theirs--not mine. You\nmust admit that there’s a difference between stealing a diamond necklace\nfor yourself and being hired to steal it.”"}, {"paragraph": 79, "text": "“There wouldn’t be the least difference if you were caught!”"}, {"paragraph": 80, "text": "“Perhaps not. But I shouldn’t be caught. I’m so clever.”"}, {"paragraph": 81, "text": "“Modesty always was your besetting sin,” remarked Tommy."}, {"paragraph": 82, "text": "“Don’t rag. Look here, Tommy, shall we really? Shall we form a business\npartnership?”"}, {"paragraph": 83, "text": "“Form a company for the stealing of diamond necklaces?”"}, {"paragraph": 84, "text": "“That was only an illustration. Let’s have a--what do you call it in\nbook-keeping?”"}, {"paragraph": 85, "text": "“Don’t know. Never did any.”"}, {"paragraph": 86, "text": "“I have--but I always got mixed up, and used to put credit entries on\nthe debit side, and vice versa--so they fired me out. Oh, I know--a\njoint venture! It struck me as such a romantic phrase to come across in\nthe middle of musty old figures. It’s got an Elizabethan flavour about\nit--makes one think of galleons and doubloons. A joint venture!”"}, {"paragraph": 87, "text": "“Trading under the name of the Young Adventurers, Ltd.? Is that your\nidea, Tuppence?”"}, {"paragraph": 88, "text": "“It’s all very well to laugh, but I feel there might be something in\nit.”"}, {"paragraph": 89, "text": "“How do you propose to get in touch with your would-be employers?”"}, {"paragraph": 90, "text": "“Advertisement,” replied Tuppence promptly. “Have you got a bit of paper\nand a pencil? Men usually seem to have. Just like we have hairpins and\npowder-puffs.”"}, {"paragraph": 91, "text": "Tommy handed over a rather shabby green notebook, and Tuppence began\nwriting busily."}, {"paragraph": 92, "text": "“Shall we begin: ‘Young officer, twice wounded in the war----’”"}, {"paragraph": 93, "text": "“Certainly not.”"}, {"paragraph": 94, "text": "“Oh, very well, my dear boy. But I can assure you that that sort of\nthing might touch the heart of an elderly spinster, and she might adopt\nyou, and then there would be no need for you to be a young adventurer at\nall.”"}, {"paragraph": 95, "text": "“I don’t want to be adopted.”"}, {"paragraph": 96, "text": "“I forgot you had a prejudice against it. Pay must be good.’ (We might as well make\nthat clear from the start.) Then we might add: ‘No reasonable offer\nrefused’--like flats and furniture.”"}, {"paragraph": 97, "text": "“I should think any offer we get in answer to that would be a pretty\n_un_reasonable one!”"}, {"paragraph": 98, "text": "“Tommy! You’re a genius! That’s ever so much more chic. ‘No unreasonable\noffer refused--if pay is good.’ How’s that?”"}, {"paragraph": 99, "text": "“I shouldn’t mention pay again. It looks rather eager.”"}, {"paragraph": 100, "text": "“It couldn’t look as eager as I feel! But perhaps you are right. Now\nI’ll read it straight through. ‘Two young adventurers for hire. Willing\nto do anything, go anywhere. Pay must be good. No unreasonable offer\nrefused.’ How would that strike you if you read it?”"}, {"paragraph": 101, "text": "“It would strike me as either being a hoax, or else written by a\nlunatic.”"}, {"paragraph": 102, "text": "“It’s not half so insane as a thing I read this morning beginning\n‘Petunia’ and signed ‘Best Boy.’” She tore out the leaf and handed it\nto Tommy. “There you are. _Times_, I think. Reply to Box so-and-so.\nI expect it will be about five shillings. Here’s half a crown for my\nshare.”"}, {"paragraph": 103, "text": "Tommy was holding the paper thoughtfully. His faced burned a deeper red."}, {"paragraph": 104, "text": "“Shall we really try it?” he said at last. “Shall we, Tuppence? Just for\nthe fun of the thing?”"}, {"paragraph": 105, "text": "“Tommy, you’re a sport! I knew you would be! Let’s drink to success.”\n She poured some cold dregs of tea into the two cups."}, {"paragraph": 106, "text": "“Here’s to our joint venture, and may it prosper!”"}, {"paragraph": 107, "text": "“The Young Adventurers, Ltd.!” responded Tommy."}, {"paragraph": 108, "text": "They put down the cups and laughed rather uncertainly. Tuppence rose."}, {"paragraph": 109, "text": "“I must return to my palatial suite at the hostel.”"}, {"paragraph": 110, "text": "“Perhaps it is time I strolled round to the _Ritz_,” agreed Tommy with a\ngrin. “Where shall we meet? And when?”"}, {"paragraph": 111, "text": "“Twelve o’clock to-morrow. Piccadilly Tube station. Will that suit you?”"}, {"paragraph": 112, "text": "“My time is my own,” replied Mr. Beresford magnificently."}, {"paragraph": 113, "text": "“So long, then.”"}, {"paragraph": 114, "text": "“Good-bye, old thing.”"}, {"paragraph": 115, "text": "The two young people went off in opposite directions. I--never heard of her!”"}, {"paragraph": 38, "text": "“You’re a darned liar! You know perfectly who I mean.”"}, {"paragraph": 39, "text": "“I tell you I’ve never heard of the girl.”"}, {"paragraph": 40, "text": "“And I tell you,” retorted Julius, “that Little Willie here is just\nhopping mad to go off!”"}, {"paragraph": 41, "text": "The Russian wilted visibly."}, {"paragraph": 42, "text": "“You wouldn’t dare----”"}, {"paragraph": 43, "text": "“Oh, yes, I would, son!”"}, {"paragraph": 44, "text": "Kramenin must have recognized something in the voice that carried\nconviction, for he said sullenly:"}, {"paragraph": 45, "text": "“Well? You ask an impossibility.”"}, {"paragraph": 51, "text": "“Afraid, eh? Of whom? Mr. Brown? Ah, that tickles you up! There is such\na person, then? I doubted it. And the mere mention of him scares you\nstiff!”"}, {"paragraph": 52, "text": "“I have seen him,” said the Russian slowly. “Spoken to him face to face.\nI did not know it until afterwards. He was one of a crowd. I should not\nknow him again. Who is he really? I do not know. But I know this--he is\na man to fear.”"}, {"paragraph": 53, "text": "“He’ll never know,” said Julius."}, {"paragraph": 54, "text": "“He knows everything--and his vengeance is swift. Even\nI--Kramenin!--would not be exempt!”"}, {"paragraph": 55, "text": "“Then you won’t do as I ask you?”"}, {"paragraph": 56, "text": "“You ask an impossibility.”"}, {"paragraph": 57, "text": "“Sure that’s a pity for you,” said Julius cheerfully. “But the world in\ngeneral will benefit.” He raised the revolver."}, {"paragraph": 58, "text": "“Stop,” shrieked the Russian. “You cannot mean to shoot me?”"}, {"paragraph": 59, "text": "“Of course I do. I’ve always heard you Revolutionists held life cheap,\nbut it seems there’s a difference when it’s your own life in question.\nI gave you just one chance of saving your dirty skin, and that you\nwouldn’t take!”"}, {"paragraph": 60, "text": "“They would kill me!”"}, {"paragraph": 61, "text": "“Well,” said Julius pleasantly, “it’s up to you. But I’ll just say this.\nLittle Willie here is a dead cert, and if I was you I’d take a sporting\nchance with Mr. Brown!”"}, {"paragraph": 62, "text": "“You will hang if you shoot me,” muttered the Russian irresolutely."}, {"paragraph": 63, "text": "“No, stranger, that’s where you’re wrong. I will do all you wish.”"}, {"paragraph": 68, "text": "Julius lowered the revolver."}, {"paragraph": 69, "text": "“I thought you’d hear sense. Where is the girl?”"}, {"paragraph": 70, "text": "“At Gatehouse, in Kent. Astley Priors, the place is called.”"}, {"paragraph": 71, "text": "“Is she a prisoner there?”"}, {"paragraph": 72, "text": "“She’s not allowed to leave the house--though it’s safe enough really.\nThe little fool has lost her memory, curse her!”"}, {"paragraph": 73, "text": "“That’s been annoying for you and your friends, I reckon. What about the\nother girl, the one you decoyed away over a week ago?”"}, {"paragraph": 74, "text": "“She’s there too,” said the Russian sullenly."}, {"paragraph": 75, "text": "“That’s good,” said Julius. “Isn’t it all panning out beautifully? The\ndanger-zone was passed. Fear had successfully hypnotized the man by his\nside."}, {"paragraph": 82, "text": "“Get in,” he ordered. Then as he caught the other’s sidelong glance,\n“No, the chauffeur won’t help you any. Naval man. Was on a submarine in\nRussia when the Revolution broke out. A brother of his was murdered by\nyour people. George!”"}, {"paragraph": 83, "text": "“Yes, sir?” The chauffeur turned his head."}, {"paragraph": 84, "text": "“This gentleman is a Russian Bolshevik. We don’t want to shoot him, but\nit may be necessary. You understand?”"}, {"paragraph": 85, "text": "“Perfectly, sir.”"}, {"paragraph": 86, "text": "“I want to go to Gatehouse in Kent. Know the road at all?”"}, {"paragraph": 87, "text": "“Yes, sir, it will be about an hour and a half’s run.”"}, {"paragraph": 88, "text": "“Make it an hour. I’m in a hurry.”"}, {"paragraph": 89, "text": "“I’ll do my best, sir.” The car shot forward through the traffic."}, {"paragraph": 90, "text": "Julius ensconced himself comfortably by the side of his victim. He kept\nhis hand in the pocket of his coat, but his manner was urbane to the\nlast degree."}, {"paragraph": 91, "text": "“There was a man I shot once in Arizona----” he began cheerfully."}, {"paragraph": 92, "text": "At the end of the hour’s run the unfortunate Kramenin was more dead than\nalive. In succession to the anecdote of the Arizona man, there had been\na tough from ‘Frisco, and an episode in the Rockies. Julius’s narrative\nstyle, if not strictly accurate, was picturesque!"}, {"paragraph": 93, "text": "Slowing down, the chauffeur called over his shoulder that they were just\ncoming into Gatehouse. Julius explained to him that Little Willie would not be tolerant\nof failure. Kramenin, by this time, was as putty in the other’s hands.\nThe terrific pace they had come had still further unmanned him. He had\ngiven himself up for dead at every corner."}, {"paragraph": 94, "text": "The car swept up the drive, and stopped before the porch. The chauffeur\nlooked round for orders."}, {"paragraph": 95, "text": "“Turn the car first, George. Then ring the bell, and get back to your\nplace. Keep the engine going, and be ready to scoot like hell when I\ngive the word.”"}, {"paragraph": 96, "text": "“Very good, sir.”"}, {"paragraph": 97, "text": "The front door was opened by the butler. Kramenin felt the muzzle of the\nrevolver pressed against his ribs."}, {"paragraph": 98, "text": "“Now,” hissed Julius. “And be careful.”"}, {"paragraph": 99, "text": "The Russian beckoned. His lips were white, and his voice was not very\nsteady:"}, {"paragraph": 100, "text": "“It is I--Kramenin! Bring down the girl at once! There is no time to\nlose!”"}, {"paragraph": 101, "text": "Whittington had come down the steps. He uttered an exclamation of\nastonishment at seeing the other."}, {"paragraph": 102, "text": "“You! What’s up? Surely you know the plan----”"}, {"paragraph": 103, "text": "Kramenin interrupted him, using the words that have created many\nunnecessary panics:"}, {"paragraph": 104, "text": "“We have been betrayed! Plans must be abandoned. We must save our own\nskins. The girl! And at once! It’s our only chance.”"}, {"paragraph": 105, "text": "Whittington hesitated, but for hardly a moment."}, {"paragraph": 106, "text": "“You have orders--from _him?_”"}, {"paragraph": 107, "text": "“Naturally! Should I be here otherwise? Hurry! There is no time to be\nlost. The other little fool had better come too.”"}, {"paragraph": 108, "text": "Whittington turned and ran back into the house. The agonizing minutes\nwent by. Then--two figures hastily huddled in cloaks appeared on the\nsteps and were hustled into the car. The smaller of the two was inclined\nto resist and Whittington shoved her in unceremoniously. Julius leaned\nforward, and in doing so the light from the open door lit up his face.\nAnother man on the steps behind Whittington gave a startled exclamation.\nConcealment was at an end."}, {"paragraph": 109, "text": "“Get a move on, George,” shouted Julius."}, {"paragraph": 110, "text": "The chauffeur slipped in his clutch, and with a bound the car started."}, {"paragraph": 111, "text": "The man on the steps uttered an oath. His hand went to his pocket. There\nwas a flash and a report. The bullet just missed the taller girl by an\ninch."}, {"paragraph": 112, "text": "“Get down, Jane,” cried Julius. “Flat on the bottom of the car.” He\nthrust her sharply forward, then standing up, he took careful aim and\nfired."}, {"paragraph": 113, "text": "“Have you hit him?” cried Tuppence eagerly."}, {"paragraph": 114, "text": "“Sure,” replied Julius. “He isn’t killed, though. Steady through the gate, George! That’s right.\nIt’ll take ‘em at least five minutes to get busy after us. They’ll use\nthe telephone, I guess, so look out for snares ahead--and don’t take the\ndirect route. Who’s this, did you say, Tuppence? Let me present Monsieur\nKramenin. He burst out vehemently:"}, {"paragraph": 121, "text": "“Curse you--curse you! They know now that I betrayed them. My life won’t\nbe safe for an hour in this country.”"}, {"paragraph": 122, "text": "“That’s so,” assented Julius. “I’d advise you to make tracks for Russia\nright away.”"}, {"paragraph": 123, "text": "“Let me go, then,” cried the other. “I have done what you asked. Why do\nyou still keep me with you?”"}, {"paragraph": 124, "text": "“Not for the pleasure of your company. I guess you can get right off now\nif you want to. I thought you’d rather I tooled you back to London.”"}, {"paragraph": 125, "text": "“You may never reach London,” snarled the other. “Let me go here and\nnow.”"}, {"paragraph": 126, "text": "“Sure thing. Pull up, George. The gentleman’s not making the return\ntrip. If I ever come to Russia, Monsieur Kramenin, I shall expect a\nrousing welcome, and----”"}, {"paragraph": 127, "text": "But before Julius had finished his speech, and before the car had\nfinally halted, the Russian had swung himself out and disappeared into\nthe night."}, {"paragraph": 128, "text": "“Just a mite impatient to leave us,” commented Julius, as the car\ngathered way again. “And no idea of saying good-bye politely to the\nladies. The colour surged into her face, her eyes\nlooked admiringly at Julius."}, {"paragraph": 134, "text": "“Annette and I didn’t know what was going to happen to us,” said\nTuppence. “Old Whittington hurried us off. _We_ thought it was lambs to\nthe slaughter.”"}, {"paragraph": 135, "text": "“Annette,” said Julius. “Is that what you call her?”"}, {"paragraph": 136, "text": "His mind seemed to be trying to adjust itself to a new idea."}, {"paragraph": 137, "text": "“It’s her name,” said Tuppence, opening her eyes very wide."}, {"paragraph": 138, "text": "“Shucks!” retorted Julius. “She may think it’s her name, because her\nmemory’s gone, poor kid. With an angry spurt, a bullet embedded itself\nin the upholstery of the car just behind her head."}, {"paragraph": 141, "text": "“Down with you,” cried Julius. “It’s an ambush. These guys have got busy\npretty quickly. Push her a bit, George.”"}, {"paragraph": 142, "text": "The car fairly leapt forward. Three more shots rang out, but went\nhappily wide. Julius, upright, leant over the back of the car."}, {"paragraph": 143, "text": "“Nothing to shoot at,” he announced gloomily. “But I guess there’ll be\nanother little picnic soon. Ah!”"}, {"paragraph": 144, "text": "He raised his hand to his cheek."}, {"paragraph": 145, "text": "“You are hurt?” said Annette quickly."}, {"paragraph": 146, "text": "“Only a scratch.”"}, {"paragraph": 147, "text": "The girl sprang to her feet."}, {"paragraph": 148, "text": "“Let me out! The bullet just missed the taller girl by an inch."}, {"paragraph": 66, "text": "“Get down, Jane,” cried Julius. “Flat on the bottom of the car.” Then, standing up, he took careful aim and fired."}, {"paragraph": 67, "text": "“Have you hit him?” cried Tuppence eagerly."}, {"paragraph": 68, "text": "“Sure,” replied Julius. “He isn’t killed, though. Are you all right, Tuppence?”"}, {"paragraph": 69, "text": "“Of course I am. Where’s Tommy? And who’s this?” She indicated the shivering Kramenin."}, {"paragraph": 70, "text": "“Tommy’s making tracks for the Argentine. I guess he thought you’d turned up your toes. Let me present Monsieur Kramenin. I persuaded him to come on the trip for his health.”"}, {"paragraph": 71, "text": "“Curse you!” burst out the Russian. “They know now that I betrayed them. Let me go. I have done what you asked.”"}, {"paragraph": 72, "text": "“Sure thing. Pull up, George.”"}, {"paragraph": 73, "text": "Before the car had finally halted, the Russian had swung himself out and disappeared into the night."}, {"paragraph": 74, "text": "“Say, Jane, you can get up on the seat now,” said Julius."}, {"paragraph": 75, "text": "For the first time the girl spoke."}, {"paragraph": 76, "text": "“How did you ‘persuade’ him?” she asked."}, {"paragraph": 77, "text": "Julius tapped his revolver."}, {"paragraph": 78, "text": "“Little Willie here takes the credit!”"}, {"paragraph": 79, "text": "“Annette and I didn’t know what was going to happen to us,” said Tuppence."}, {"paragraph": 80, "text": "“Annette,” said Julius. “Is that what you call her?”"}, {"paragraph": 81, "text": "“It’s her name,” said Tuppence, opening her eyes very wide."}, {"paragraph": 82, "text": "“Shucks!” retorted Julius. “She may think it’s her name, because her memory’s gone, poor kid. But it’s the one real and original Jane Finn we’ve got here.”"}, {"paragraph": 83, "text": "“What?” cried Tuppence."}, {"paragraph": 84, "text": "A bullet embedded itself in the upholstery just behind her head."}, {"paragraph": 85, "text": "“Down with you,” cried Julius. “It’s an ambush. Push her a bit, George.”"}, {"paragraph": 86, "text": "Three more shots rang out. Julius raised his hand to his cheek."}, {"paragraph": 87, "text": "“You are hurt?” said Annette quickly."}, {"paragraph": 88, "text": "“Only a scratch.”"}, {"paragraph": 89, "text": "The girl sprang to her feet."}, {"paragraph": 90, "text": "“Let me out! It is me they’re after. You shall not lose your lives because of me.”"}, {"paragraph": 91, "text": "Julius took her by both arms. She had spoken with no trace of foreign accent."}, {"paragraph": 92, "text": "“Sit down, kid,” he said gently. “I guess there’s nothing wrong with your memory. Been fooling them all the time, eh?”"}, {"paragraph": 93, "text": "The girl nodded, and then suddenly burst into tears."}, {"paragraph": 94, "text": "“You’re from home,” she said indistinctly. “I can tell by your voice.”"}, {"paragraph": 95, "text": "“Sure I’m from home. I’m your cousin--Julius Hersheimmer. I came over to Europe on purpose to find you.”"}, {"paragraph": 96, "text": "The car slowed at cross-roads till it hardly moved. As it did so a figure climbed suddenly over the back, and plunged head first into the midst of them."}, {"paragraph": 97, "text": "“Sorry,” said Tommy, extricating himself. “Was in the bushes by the drive. Hung on behind. Now then, you girls, get out! There’s a station just up that road. Train due in three minutes.”"}, {"paragraph": 98, "text": "“What the devil are you driving at?” demanded Julius."}, {"paragraph": 99, "text": "“You and I aren’t going to leave the car. Only the girls.”"}, {"paragraph": 100, "text": "Tommy turned to Tuppence."}, {"paragraph": 101, "text": "“Get out at once, Tuppence. Take her with you, and do just as I say. You’re safe. Take the train to London. Go straight to Sir James Peel Edgerton.”"}, {"paragraph": 102, "text": "“Darn you!” cried Julius. “Jane, you stay where you are.”"}, {"paragraph": 103, "text": "With a sudden swift movement, Tommy snatched the revolver from Julius’s hand, and levelled it at him."}, {"paragraph": 104, "text": "“Now will you believe I’m in earnest? Get out, both of you--or I’ll shoot!”"}, {"paragraph": 105, "text": "Tuppence sprang out, dragging the unwilling Jane after her."}, {"paragraph": 106, "text": "“Come on, it’s all right. If Tommy’s sure--he’s sure. Be quick.”"}, {"paragraph": 107, "text": "They started running. Julius’s pent-up rage burst forth."}, {"paragraph": 108, "text": "“What the hell----”"}, {"paragraph": 109, "text": "Tommy interrupted him."}, {"paragraph": 110, "text": "“Dry up! I want a few words with you, Mr. Julius Hersheimmer.”"}], "028.source": [{"paragraph": 1, "text": "THE supper party given by Mr. Julius Hersheimmer to a few friends on the\nevening of the 30th will long be remembered in catering circles. It took\nplace in a private room, and Mr. Hersheimmer’s orders were brief and\nforcible. He gave carte blanche--and when a millionaire gives carte\nblanche he usually gets it!"}, {"paragraph": 2, "text": "Every delicacy out of season was duly provided. Waiters carried bottles\nof ancient and royal vintage with loving care. The floral decorations\ndefied the seasons, and fruits of the earth as far apart as May and\nNovember found themselves miraculously side by side. The list of guests\nwas small and select. The American Ambassador, Mr. Carter, who had taken\nthe liberty, he said, of bringing an old friend, Sir William Beresford,\nwith him, Archdeacon Cowley, Dr. Hall, those two youthful adventurers,\nMiss Prudence Cowley and Mr. Thomas Beresford, and last, but not least,\nas guest of honour, Miss Jane Finn."}, {"paragraph": 3, "text": "Julius had spared no pains to make Jane’s appearance a success. A\nmysterious knock had brought Tuppence to the door of the apartment she\nwas sharing with the American girl. It was Julius. In his hand he held a\ncheque."}, {"paragraph": 4, "text": "“Say, Tuppence,” he began, “will you do me a good turn? Take this, and\nget Jane regularly togged up for this evening. You’re all coming to\nsupper with me at the _Savoy_. See? Spare no expense. You get me?”"}, {"paragraph": 5, "text": "“Sure thing,” mimicked Tuppence. “We shall enjoy ourselves. It will be a\npleasure dressing Jane. She’s the loveliest thing I’ve ever seen.”"}, {"paragraph": 6, "text": "“That’s so,” agreed Mr. Hersheimmer fervently."}, {"paragraph": 7, "text": "His fervour brought a momentary twinkle to Tuppence’s eye."}, {"paragraph": 8, "text": "“By the way, Julius,” she remarked demurely, “I--haven’t given you my\nanswer yet.”"}, {"paragraph": 9, "text": "“Answer?” said Julius. His face paled."}, {"paragraph": 10, "text": "“You know--when you asked me to--marry you,” faltered Tuppence, her\neyes downcast in the true manner of the early Victorian heroine, “and\nwouldn’t take no for an answer. I’ve thought it well over----”"}, {"paragraph": 11, "text": "“Yes?” said Julius. The perspiration stood on his forehead."}, {"paragraph": 12, "text": "Tuppence relented suddenly."}, {"paragraph": 13, "text": "“You great idiot!” she said. “What on earth induced you to do it? I\ncould see at the time you didn’t care a twopenny dip for me!”"}, {"paragraph": 14, "text": "“Not at all. I had--and still have--the highest sentiments of esteem and\nrespect--and admiration for you----”"}, {"paragraph": 15, "text": "“H’m!” said Tuppence. “Those are the kind of sentiments that very soon\ngo to the wall when the other sentiment comes along! Don’t they, old\nthing?”"}, {"paragraph": 16, "text": "“I don’t know what you mean,” said Julius stiffly, but a large and\nburning blush overspread his countenance."}, {"paragraph": 17, "text": "“Shucks!” retorted Tuppence. She laughed, and closed the door, reopening\nit to add with dignity: “Morally, I shall always consider I have been\njilted!”"}, {"paragraph": 18, "text": "“What was it?” asked Jane as Tuppence rejoined her."}, {"paragraph": 19, "text": "“Julius.”"}, {"paragraph": 20, "text": "“What did he want?”"}, {"paragraph": 21, "text": "“Really, I think, he wanted to see you, but I wasn’t going to let him.\nNot until to-night, when you’re going to burst upon every one like King\nSolomon in his glory! Come on! _We’re going to shop!_”"}, {"paragraph": 22, "text": "To most people the 29th, the much-heralded “Labour Day,” had passed much\nas any other day. Speeches were made in the Park and Trafalgar Square.\nStraggling processions, singing the _Red Flag_, wandered through the\nstreets in a more or less aimless manner. Newspapers which had hinted at\na general strike, and the inauguration of a reign of terror, were forced\nto hide their diminished heads. The bolder and more astute among\nthem sought to prove that peace had been effected by following their\ncounsels. In the Sunday papers a brief notice of the sudden death of Sir\nJames Peel Edgerton, the famous K.C., had appeared. Monday’s paper\ndealt appreciatively with the dead man’s career. The exact manner of his\nsudden death was never made public."}, {"paragraph": 23, "text": "Tommy had been right in his forecast of the situation. It had been a\none-man show. Deprived of their chief, the organization fell to pieces.\nKramenin had made a precipitate return to Russia, leaving England early\non Sunday morning. The gang had fled from Astley Priors in a panic,\nleaving behind, in their haste, various damaging documents which\ncompromised them hopelessly. With these proofs of conspiracy in their\nhands, aided further by a small brown diary taken from the pocket of the\ndead man which had contained a full and damning résumé of the whole\nplot, the Government had called an eleventh-hour conference. The Labour\nleaders were forced to recognize that they had been used as a cat’s\npaw. Certain concessions were made by the Government, and were eagerly\naccepted. It was to be Peace, not War!"}, {"paragraph": 24, "text": "But the Cabinet knew by how narrow a margin they had escaped utter\ndisaster. And burnt in on Mr. Carter’s brain was the strange scene which\nhad taken place in the house in Soho the night before."}, {"paragraph": 25, "text": "He had entered the squalid room to find that great man, the friend of\na lifetime, dead--betrayed out of his own mouth. From the dead man’s\npocket-book he had retrieved the ill-omened draft treaty, and then\nand there, in the presence of the other three, it had been reduced to\nashes.... England was saved!"}, {"paragraph": 26, "text": "And now, on the evening of the 30th, in a private room at the _Savoy_,\nMr. Julius P. Hersheimmer was receiving his guests."}, {"paragraph": 27, "text": "Mr. Carter was the first to arrive. With him was a choleric-looking old\ngentleman, at sight of whom Tommy flushed up to the roots of his hair.\nHe came forward."}, {"paragraph": 28, "text": "“Ha!” said the old gentleman, surveying him apoplectically. “So you’re\nmy nephew, are you? Not much to look at--but you’ve done good work, it\nseems. Your mother must have brought you up well after all. Shall we\nlet bygones be bygones, eh? You’re my heir, you know; and in future I\npropose to make you an allowance--and you can look upon Chalmers Park as\nyour home.”"}, {"paragraph": 29, "text": "“Thank you, sir, it’s awfully decent of you.”"}, {"paragraph": 30, "text": "“Where’s this young lady I’ve been hearing such a lot about?”"}, {"paragraph": 31, "text": "Tommy introduced Tuppence."}, {"paragraph": 32, "text": "“Ha!” said Sir William, eyeing her. “Girls aren’t what they used to be\nin my young days.”"}, {"paragraph": 33, "text": "“Yes, they are,” said Tuppence. “Their clothes are different, perhaps,\nbut they themselves are just the same.”"}, {"paragraph": 34, "text": "“Well, perhaps you’re right. Minxes then--minxes now!”"}, {"paragraph": 35, "text": "“That’s it,” said Tuppence. “I’m a frightful minx myself.”"}, {"paragraph": 36, "text": "“I believe you,” said the old gentleman, chuckling, and pinched her ear\nin high good-humour. Most young women were terrified of the “old bear,”\n as they termed him. Tuppence’s pertness delighted the old misogynist."}, {"paragraph": 37, "text": "Then came the timid archdeacon, a little bewildered by the company in\nwhich he found himself, glad that his daughter was considered to have\ndistinguished herself, but unable to help glancing at her from time\nto time with nervous apprehension. But Tuppence behaved admirably. She\nforbore to cross her legs, set a guard upon her tongue, and steadfastly\nrefused to smoke."}, {"paragraph": 38, "text": "Dr. Hall came next, and he was followed by the American Ambassador."}, {"paragraph": 39, "text": "“We might as well sit down,” said Julius, when he had introduced all his\nguests to each other. “Tuppence, will you----”"}, {"paragraph": 40, "text": "He indicated the place of honour with a wave of his hand."}, {"paragraph": 41, "text": "But Tuppence shook her head."}, {"paragraph": 42, "text": "“No--that’s Jane’s place! When one thinks of how she’s held out all\nthese years, she ought to be made the queen of the feast to-night.”"}, {"paragraph": 43, "text": "Julius flung her a grateful glance, and Jane came forward shyly to the\nallotted seat. Beautiful as she had seemed before, it was as nothing to\nthe loveliness that now went fully adorned. Tuppence had performed her\npart faithfully. The model gown supplied by a famous dressmaker had been\nentitled “A tiger lily.” It was all golds and reds and browns, and out\nof it rose the pure column of the girl’s white throat, and the bronze\nmasses of hair that crowned her lovely head. There was admiration in\nevery eye, as she took her seat."}, {"paragraph": 44, "text": "Soon the supper party was in full swing, and with one accord Tommy was\ncalled upon for a full and complete explanation."}, {"paragraph": 45, "text": "“You’ve been too darned close about the whole business,” Julius accused\nhim. “You let on to me that you were off to the Argentine--though I\nguess you had your reasons for that. The idea of both you and Tuppence\ncasting me for the part of Mr. Brown just tickles me to death!”"}, {"paragraph": 46, "text": "“The idea was not original to them,” said Mr. Carter gravely. “It was\nsuggested, and the poison very carefully instilled, by a past-master in\nthe art. The paragraph in the New York paper suggested the plan to him,\nand by means of it he wove a web that nearly enmeshed you fatally.”"}, {"paragraph": 47, "text": "“I never liked him,” said Julius. “I felt from the first that there was\nsomething wrong about him, and I always suspected that it was he who\nsilenced Mrs. Vandemeyer so appositely. But it wasn’t till I heard that\nthe order for Tommy’s execution came right on the heels of our interview\nwith him that Sunday that I began to tumble to the fact that he was the\nbig bug himself.”"}, {"paragraph": 48, "text": "“I never suspected it at all,” lamented Tuppence. “I’ve always thought\nI was so much cleverer than Tommy--but he’s undoubtedly scored over me\nhandsomely.”"}, {"paragraph": 49, "text": "Julius agreed."}, {"paragraph": 50, "text": "“Tommy’s been the goods this trip! And, instead of sitting there as dumb\nas a fish, let him banish his blushes, and tell us all about it.”"}, {"paragraph": 51, "text": "“Hear! hear!”"}, {"paragraph": 52, "text": "“There’s nothing to tell,” said Tommy, acutely uncomfortable. “I was an\nawful mug--right up to the time I found that photograph of Annette, and\nrealized that she was Jane Finn. Then I remembered how persistently she\nhad shouted out that word ‘Marguerite’--and I thought of the pictures,\nand--well, that’s that. Then of course I went over the whole thing to\nsee where I’d made an ass of myself.”"}, {"paragraph": 53, "text": "“Go on,” said Mr. Carter, as Tommy showed signs of taking refuge in\nsilence once more."}, {"paragraph": 54, "text": "“That business about Mrs. Vandemeyer had worried me when Julius told me\nabout it. On the face of it, it seemed that he or Sir James must have\ndone the trick. But I didn’t know which. Finding that photograph in the\ndrawer, after that story of how it had been got from him by Inspector\nBrown, made me suspect Julius. Then I remembered that it was Sir James\nwho had discovered the false Jane Finn. In the end, I couldn’t make up\nmy mind--and just decided to take no chances either way. I left a note\nfor Julius, in case he was Mr. Brown, saying I was off to the Argentine,\nand I dropped Sir James’s letter with the offer of the job by the desk\nso that he would see it was a genuine stunt. Then I wrote my letter to\nMr. Carter and rang up Sir James. Taking him into my confidence would\nbe the best thing either way, so I told him everything except where I\nbelieved the papers to be hidden. The way he helped me to get on the\ntrack of Tuppence and Annette almost disarmed me, but not quite. I kept\nmy mind open between the two of them. And then I got a bogus note from\nTuppence--and I knew!”"}, {"paragraph": 55, "text": "“But how?”"}, {"paragraph": 56, "text": "Tommy took the note in question from his pocket and passed it round the\ntable."}, {"paragraph": 57, "text": "“It’s her handwriting all right, but I knew it wasn’t from her because\nof the signature. She’d never spell her name ‘Twopence,’ but anyone\nwho’d never seen it written might quite easily do so. Julius _had_ seen\nit--he showed me a note of hers to him once--but _Sir James hadn’t!_\nAfter that everything was plain sailing. I sent off Albert post-haste to\nMr. Carter. I pretended to go away, but doubled back again. When Julius\ncame bursting up in his car, I felt it wasn’t part of Mr. Brown’s\nplan--and that there would probably be trouble. Unless Sir James was\nactually caught in the act, so to speak, I knew Mr. Carter would never\nbelieve it of him on my bare word----”"}, {"paragraph": 58, "text": "“I didn’t,” interposed Mr. Carter ruefully."}, {"paragraph": 59, "text": "“That’s why I sent the girls off to Sir James. I was sure they’d fetch\nup at the house in Soho sooner or later. I threatened Julius with the\nrevolver, because I wanted Tuppence to repeat that to Sir James, so that\nhe wouldn’t worry about us. The moment the girls were out of sight I\ntold Julius to drive like hell for London, and as we went along I told\nhim the whole story. We got to the Soho house in plenty of time and met\nMr. Carter outside. After arranging things with him we went in and hid\nbehind the curtain in the recess. The policemen had orders to say, if\nthey were asked, that no one had gone into the house. That’s all.”"}, {"paragraph": 60, "text": "And Tommy came to an abrupt halt."}, {"paragraph": 61, "text": "There was silence for a moment."}, {"paragraph": 62, "text": "“By the way,” said Julius suddenly, “you’re all wrong about that\nphotograph of Jane. It _was_ taken from me, but I found it again.”"}, {"paragraph": 63, "text": "“Where?” cried Tuppence."}, {"paragraph": 64, "text": "“In that little safe on the wall in Mrs. Vandemeyer’s bedroom.”"}, {"paragraph": 65, "text": "“I knew you found something,” said Tuppence reproachfully. “To tell you\nthe truth, that’s what started me off suspecting you. Why didn’t you\nsay?”"}, {"paragraph": 66, "text": "“I guess I was a mite suspicious too. It had been got away from me once,\nand I determined I wouldn’t let on I’d got it until a photographer had\nmade a dozen copies of it!”"}, {"paragraph": 67, "text": "“We all kept back something or other,” said Tuppence thoughtfully. “I\nsuppose secret service work makes you like that!”"}, {"paragraph": 68, "text": "In the pause that ensued, Mr. Carter took from his pocket a small shabby\nbrown book."}, {"paragraph": 69, "text": "“Beresford has just said that I would not have believed Sir James Peel\nEdgerton to be guilty unless, so to speak, he was caught in the act.\nThat is so. Indeed, not until I read the entries in this little book\ncould I bring myself fully to credit the amazing truth. This book will\npass into the possession of Scotland Yard, but it will never be publicly\nexhibited. Sir James’s long association with the law would make it\nundesirable. But to you, who know the truth, I propose to read certain\npassages which will throw some light on the extraordinary mentality of\nthis great man.”"}, {"paragraph": 70, "text": "He opened the book, and turned the thin pages."}, {"paragraph": 71, "text": "“... It is madness to keep this book. I know that. It is documentary\nevidence against me. But I have never shrunk from taking risks. And I\nfeel an urgent need for self-expression.... The book will only be taken\nfrom my dead body...."}, {"paragraph": 72, "text": "“... From an early age I realized that I had exceptional abilities. Only\na fool underestimates his capabilities. My brain power was greatly above\nthe average. I know that I was born to succeed. My appearance was\nthe only thing against me. I was quiet and insignificant--utterly\nnondescript...."}, {"paragraph": 73, "text": "“... When I was a boy I heard a famous murder trial. I was deeply\nimpressed by the power and eloquence of the counsel for the defence.\nFor the first time I entertained the idea of taking my talents to that\nparticular market.... Then I studied the criminal in the dock.... The\nman was a fool--he had been incredibly, unbelievably stupid. Even\nthe eloquence of his counsel was hardly likely to save him. I felt\nan immeasurable contempt for him.... Then it occurred to me that the\ncriminal standard was a low one. It was the wastrels, the failures, the\ngeneral riff-raff of civilization who drifted into crime....\nStrange that men of brains had never realized its extraordinary\nopportunities.... I played with the idea.... What a magnificent\nfield--what unlimited possibilities! It made my brain reel...."}, {"paragraph": 74, "text": "“... I read standard works on crime and criminals. They all confirmed my\nopinion. Degeneracy, disease--never the deliberate embracing of a career\nby a far-seeing man. Then I considered. Supposing my utmost ambitions\nwere realized--that I was called to the bar, and rose to the height of\nmy profession? That I entered politics--say, even, that I became Prime\nMinister of England? What then? Was that power? Hampered at every turn\nby my colleagues, fettered by the democratic system of which I should\nbe the mere figurehead! No--the power I dreamed of was absolute! An\nautocrat! A dictator! And such power could only be obtained by working\noutside the law. To play on the weaknesses of human nature, then on the\nweaknesses of nations--to get together and control a vast organization,\nand finally to overthrow the existing order, and rule! The thought\nintoxicated me...."}, {"paragraph": 75, "text": "“... I saw that I must lead two lives. A man like myself is bound to\nattract notice. I must have a successful career which would mask my true\nactivities.... Also I must cultivate a personality. I modelled myself\nupon famous K.C.’s. I reproduced their mannerisms, their magnetism. If I\nhad chosen to be an actor, I should have been the greatest actor living!\nNo disguises--no grease paint--no false beards! Personality! I put it\non like a glove! When I shed it, I was myself, quiet, unobtrusive, a man\nlike every other man. I called myself Mr. Brown. There are hundreds of\nmen called Brown--there are hundreds of men looking just like me...."}, {"paragraph": 76, "text": "“... I succeeded in my false career. I was bound to succeed. I shall\nsucceed in the other. A man like me cannot fail...."}, {"paragraph": 77, "text": "“... I have been reading a life of Napoleon. He and I have much in\ncommon...."}, {"paragraph": 78, "text": "“... I make a practice of defending criminals. A man should look after\nhis own people...."}, {"paragraph": 79, "text": "“... Once or twice I have felt afraid. The first time was in Italy.\nThere was a dinner given. Professor D----, the great alienist, was\npresent. The talk fell on insanity. He said, ‘A great many men are\nmad, and no one knows it. They do not know it themselves.’ I do not\nunderstand why he looked at me when he said that. His glance was\nstrange.... I did not like it...."}, {"paragraph": 80, "text": "“... The war has disturbed me.... I thought it would further my plans.\nThe Germans are so efficient. Their spy system, too, was excellent.\nThe streets are full of these boys in khaki. All empty-headed young\nfools.... Yet I do not know.... They won the war.... It disturbs me...."}, {"paragraph": 81, "text": "“... My plans are going well.... A girl butted in--I do not think she\nreally knew anything.... But we must give up the Esthonia.... No risks\nnow...."}, {"paragraph": 82, "text": "“.... All goes well. The loss of memory is vexing. It cannot be a fake.\nNo girl could deceive ME!..."}, {"paragraph": 83, "text": "“...The 29th.... That is very soon....” Mr. Carter paused."}, {"paragraph": 84, "text": "“I will not read the details of the _coup_ that was planned. But there\nare just two small entries that refer to the three of you. In the light\nof what happened they are interesting."}, {"paragraph": 85, "text": "“... By inducing the girl to come to me of her own accord, I have\nsucceeded in disarming her. But she has intuitive flashes that might be\ndangerous.... She must be got out of the way.... I can do nothing with\nthe American. He suspects and dislikes me. But he cannot know. I fancy\nmy armour is impregnable.... Sometimes I fear I have underestimated\nthe other boy. He is not clever, but it is hard to blind his eyes to\nfacts....”"}, {"paragraph": 86, "text": "Mr. Carter shut the book."}, {"paragraph": 87, "text": "“A great man,” he said. “Genius, or insanity, who can say?”"}, {"paragraph": 88, "text": "There was silence."}, {"paragraph": 89, "text": "Then Mr. Carter rose to his feet."}, {"paragraph": 90, "text": "“I will give you a toast. We’ll\nask Miss Jane Finn to tell us the story that only Miss Tuppence has\nheard so far--but before we do so we’ll drink her health.
